blocks.en: 1. What "Canon" Means — and What It Does Not
blocks.es_reference: 1. Qué Significa "Canon" — y Qué No

blocks.en: The word "canon" comes from a Greek term, kanōn, meaning a measuring reed, a rule. The canon is the list of books that are Scripture — the measure of what belongs and what does not. And here is something crucial: a book is not Scripture because a council said so; the council recognized what God had already given. The image helps. An assayer certifies gold, but he does not make it gold; the gold was precious before he arrived with his scale. In the same way, the synagogue and the church did not create the canon — they received it and recognized it. Scripture's authority is intrinsic, because it is God-breathed; recognition is the community catching up to what was already true. This flows straight out of Unit 1: authority belongs to the Word itself, not to those who acknowledge it. Hold this distinction and you will not be confused when someone says, "the church decided which books are the Bible." The church did not decide; it discerned.
blocks.es_reference: La palabra "canon" viene de un término griego, kanōn, que significa una caña de medir, una regla. El canon es la lista de libros que son Escritura — la medida de lo que pertenece y lo que no. Y aquí hay algo crucial: un libro no es Escritura porque un concilio lo dijera; el concilio reconoció lo que Dios ya había dado. La imagen ayuda. El ensayador certifica el oro, pero no lo hace oro; el oro ya era precioso antes de que él llegara con su balanza. Así también, la sinagoga y la iglesia no crearon el canon — lo recibieron y lo reconocieron. La autoridad de la Escritura es intrínseca, porque es exhalada por Dios; el reconocimiento es la comunidad alcanzando lo que ya era verdad. Esto fluye directamente de la Unidad 1: la autoridad pertenece a la Palabra misma, no a quienes la reconocen. Guarda esta distinción y no te confundirás cuando alguien diga: "la iglesia decidió cuáles libros son la Biblia." La iglesia no decidió; discernió.

blocks.en: 2. The Shape of the Hebrew Bible: Law, Prophets, Writings
blocks.es_reference: 2. La Forma de la Biblia Hebrea: Ley, Profetas, Escritos

blocks.en: The Old Testament came in three parts. First, the Law — the Torah, the five books of Moses — recognized first and earliest, placed beside the ark (Deuteronomy 31:24–26). Second, the Prophets (Nevi'im), which the Jews divided into the Former Prophets (Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings) and the Latter (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Twelve). Third, the Writings (Ketuvim), which include the Psalms, Proverbs, Job, and more. This threefold shape is old, and Jesus Himself reflects it.
blocks.es_reference: El Antiguo Testamento vino en tres partes. Primero, la Ley — la Torá, los cinco libros de Moisés — reconocida primero y más temprano, colocada al lado del arca (Deuteronomio 31:24–26). Segundo, los Profetas (Nevi'im), que los judíos dividían en los Profetas Anteriores (Josué, Jueces, Samuel, Reyes) y los Posteriores (Isaías, Jeremías, Ezequiel y los Doce). Tercero, los Escritos (Ketuvim), que incluyen los Salmos, Proverbios, Job y más. Esta forma triple es antigua, y el mismo Jesús la refleja.

blocks.en: "...all things must be fulfilled which were written in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms concerning Me" (Luke 24:44).
blocks.es_reference: "...era necesario que se cumpliese todo lo que está escrito de mí en la ley de Moisés, y en los profetas, y en los salmos" (Lucas 24:44).

blocks.en: The Psalms, the first and largest book of the Writings, stand for that whole third part. These are the same books we have, grouped in another way. When Jesus named the three parts, He was describing a Hebrew Bible already known and settled.
blocks.es_reference: Los Salmos, el primer y mayor libro de los Escritos, representan toda esa tercera parte. Son los mismos libros que tenemos, agrupados de otra manera. Cuando Jesús nombró las tres partes, describía una Biblia hebrea ya conocida y establecida.

blocks.en: 3. How the Books Were Recognized
blocks.es_reference: 3. Cómo Fueron Reconocidos los Libros

blocks.en: How did these books come to be recognized as Scripture? Not by a vote on a date, but over time, by certain marks. A book carried authority if it came from a prophet or under prophetic authority — a spokesman to whom God had spoken. It agreed with what God had already revealed; it did not contradict the Word given before. It bore the unmistakable ring of God's own voice, which His people learned to know. And it was received and used by the covenant community across the generations. The Law was recognized in Moses' day; the Prophets, as they came; the Writings, gathered over time. Recognition was a settling, not a manufacturing. No one sat down to invent which books would be holy; the people of God recognized the voice already speaking in them, the way a sheep knows the voice of its shepherd.
blocks.es_reference: ¿Cómo llegaron estos libros a ser reconocidos como Escritura? No por una votación en una fecha, sino con el tiempo, por ciertas marcas. Un libro llevaba autoridad si venía de un profeta o bajo autoridad profética — un portavoz al que Dios había hablado. Concordaba con lo que Dios ya había revelado; no contradecía la Palabra dada antes. Tenía el timbre inconfundible de la voz de Dios, que su pueblo aprendía a conocer. Y era recibido y usado por la comunidad del pacto a través de las generaciones. La Ley fue reconocida en los días de Moisés; los Profetas, conforme venían; los Escritos, reunidos con el tiempo. El reconocimiento fue un asentarse, no una fabricación. Nadie se sentó a inventar cuáles libros serían sagrados; el pueblo de Dios reconoció la voz que ya hablaba en ellos, así como una oveja conoce la voz de su pastor.

blocks.en: 4. The Canon Jesus Held
blocks.es_reference: 4. El Canon que Jesús Tenía

blocks.en: Jesus and the apostles received a settled Hebrew canon and treated it as the Word that cannot be broken: "the Scripture cannot be broken" (John 10:35); "It is written." And Jesus marked its edges. In Luke 11:51 He speaks of the blood of the martyrs "from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah" — the first and the last murders in the Hebrew Bible's own order (Genesis to Chronicles, since Chronicles stands last in the Hebrew arrangement). It is like saying "from Genesis to Revelation": He drew a line around the whole Hebrew Scriptures. The Old Testament was already fixed when He taught from it. He was not completing it or correcting it; He took it for granted as the settled Word of God, and He called His hearers to submit to it.
blocks.es_reference: Jesús y los apóstoles recibieron un canon hebreo ya establecido y lo trataron como la Palabra que no se puede quebrantar: "la Escritura no puede ser quebrantada" (Juan 10:35); "Escrito está." Y Jesús marcó sus bordes. En Lucas 11:51 habla de la sangre de los mártires "desde la sangre de Abel hasta la sangre de Zacarías" — el primer y el último asesinato en el orden propio de la Biblia hebrea (de Génesis a Crónicas, pues Crónicas está al final en el arreglo hebreo). Es como decir "desde Génesis hasta Apocalipsis": trazó una línea alrededor de todas las Escrituras hebreas. El Antiguo Testamento ya estaba fijado cuando Él enseñaba de él. No lo estaba completando ni corrigiendo; lo daba por sentado como la Palabra establecida de Dios, y llamaba a sus oyentes a someterse a ella.

blocks.en: 5. The Witness from Outside: Josephus
blocks.es_reference: 5. El Testimonio de Fuera: Josefo

blocks.en: We also have testimony from outside the Bible. The Jewish historian Josephus, writing about AD 95 (in Against Apion), says the Jews have a fixed number of books, written between Moses and the reign of Artaxerxes, to which nothing has been added since — and which no one dares to alter. He counts them as twenty-two. This is outside testimony that, by the first century, the Hebrew canon was closed and known — not open and still under debate. A people who did not dare to change their books were not waiting for a council to decide them.
blocks.es_reference: Tenemos también testimonio de fuera de la Biblia. El historiador judío Josefo, escribiendo cerca del año 95 d.C. (en Contra Apión), dice que los judíos tienen un número fijo de libros, escritos entre Moisés y el reinado de Artajerjes, a los que nada se ha añadido desde entonces — y que nadie se atreve a alterar. Los cuenta como veintidós. Este es un testimonio externo de que, para el primer siglo, el canon hebreo estaba cerrado y era conocido — no abierto ni todavía en debate. Un pueblo que no se atrevía a cambiar sus libros no estaba esperando un concilio para decidirlos.

blocks.en: 6. Why the Numbers Differ: 22, 24, and 39
blocks.es_reference: 6. Por Qué Difieren los Números: 22, 24 y 39

blocks.en: The believer in the pew hears "22 books," "24 books," "39 books," and wonders which is right. They are the same books, counted differently. The Hebrew tradition reached 22 (matching the letters of the Hebrew alphabet) or 24, by treating the twelve Minor Prophets as one book, and joining Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, and Ezra-Nehemiah each as single books. Our English and Spanish Bibles split those out and reach 39. Nothing is added or removed — only grouped differently. It is like counting a dozen eggs as "one" (a carton) or as "twelve" (the eggs): the contents do not change. (The Apocrypha, which is a genuinely separate question, waits for the next unit; there we will ask why some Bibles include extra books at all.)
blocks.es_reference: El creyente en la banca oye "22 libros", "24 libros", "39 libros", y se pregunta cuál es el correcto. Son los mismos libros, contados de otra manera. La tradición hebrea llegó a 22 (igualando las letras del alfabeto hebreo) o 24, tratando los doce Profetas Menores como un solo libro, y uniendo Samuel, Reyes, Crónicas y Esdras-Nehemías cada uno como libros únicos. Nuestras Biblias en español y en inglés los separan y llegan a 39. Nada se añade ni se quita — solo se agrupa distinto. Es como contar una docena de huevos como "uno" (un cartón) o como "doce" (los huevos): el contenido no cambia. (Los libros apócrifos, que son una cuestión verdaderamente aparte, esperan a la próxima unidad; allí preguntaremos por qué algunas Biblias incluyen libros adicionales.)

blocks.en: 7. A Camel Worth Refusing: The "Council of Jamnia"
blocks.es_reference: 7. Un Camello que Vale Rechazar: El "Concilio de Jamnia"

blocks.en: We do not swallow a claim because it is familiar. We test it.
blocks.es_reference: No tragamos una afirmación porque sea familiar. La probamos.

blocks.en: Here the unit applies its own rule. For a long time it was widely taught — in classrooms, from pulpits, in good faith — that the Old Testament canon was closed by a Jewish council at Jamnia (Yavneh) about AD 90. Whole generations of students were handed that claim on a trusted teacher's word and never checked it. But when you go looking for that council, you do not find it. The idea traces to a nineteenth-century scholar's reconstruction, not to any ancient record. What the rabbis at Yavneh actually discussed was whether books like Ecclesiastes and Song of Songs "defile the hands" — and that very discussion assumes the books were already treated as Scripture. There was no committee that met to decide the canon. And notice: correcting the error does not weaken the conservative case — it strengthens it. The truth is not "a late Jewish council voted the canon in"; the truth is that the canon was recognized far earlier and needed no council to make it so. This is exactly the discipline of Unit 1: we do not swallow a claim because it is familiar; we test it, and we let the evidence lead us to the more honest — and here, the more conservative — conclusion.
blocks.es_reference: Aquí la unidad aplica su propia regla. Por mucho tiempo se enseñó ampliamente — en aulas, desde púlpitos, de buena fe — que el canon del Antiguo Testamento fue cerrado por un concilio judío en Jamnia (Yavne) alrededor del año 90 d.C. Generaciones enteras de estudiantes recibieron esa afirmación por la palabra de un maestro de confianza y nunca la comprobaron. Pero cuando uno va a buscar ese concilio, no lo encuentra. La idea proviene de la reconstrucción de un erudito del siglo XIX, no de ningún registro antiguo. Lo que los rabinos en Yavne en verdad discutieron fue si libros como Eclesiastés y el Cantar de los Cantares "contaminan las manos" — y esa misma discusión supone que los libros ya se trataban como Escritura. No hubo comité que se reuniera a decidir el canon. Y observa: corregir el error no debilita la posición conservadora — la fortalece. La verdad no es "un concilio judío tardío votó el canon"; la verdad es que el canon fue reconocido mucho antes y no necesitó concilio para serlo. Esta es exactamente la disciplina de la Unidad 1: no tragamos una afirmación porque sea familiar; la probamos, y dejamos que la evidencia nos lleve a la conclusión más honesta — y aquí, la más conservadora.

blocks.en: 8. The Right Books in Your Hands
blocks.es_reference: 8. Los Libros Correctos en Tus Manos

blocks.en: So the first witness has spoken. The Old Testament in your Bible is not a later collection imposed by a council; it is the Hebrew Scriptures recognized over centuries and already settled in Jesus' day — the very books He read, quoted, and called unbreakable. When you open to Genesis, or the Psalms, or Malachi, you are holding what He held. The right books. In the next unit we turn to the New Testament — and to the honest question of the extra books some Bibles include: the Apocrypha. Do they belong? Why are they in some Bibles and not others? The second side of the first witness awaits.
blocks.es_reference: Así ha hablado el primer testigo. El Antiguo Testamento en tu Biblia no es una colección posterior impuesta por un concilio; son las Escrituras hebreas reconocidas a lo largo de los siglos y ya establecidas en tiempos de Jesús — los mismos libros que Él leyó, citó y llamó indestructibles. Cuando abres en Génesis, o en los Salmos, o en Malaquías, sostienes lo que Él sostuvo. Los libros correctos. En la próxima unidad pasamos al Nuevo Testamento — y a la pregunta honesta sobre los libros adicionales que algunas Biblias incluyen: los apócrifos. ¿Pertenecen? ¿Por qué están en unas Biblias y no en otras? El segundo lado del primer testigo nos espera.

sa.prompt: Explain the difference between the canon being "recognized" and being "conferred," and why it matters.
sa.model: The canon was recognized, not conferred: the books were already God-breathed Scripture, and the community simply recognized the authority God had given. A council no more makes a book Scripture than an assayer makes gold precious — it certifies what is already so. This matters because Scripture's authority is intrinsic, not granted by any church.

sa.prompt: Name the threefold division of the Hebrew Bible and say where Jesus reflects it.
sa.model: The Hebrew Bible came in three parts: the Law (Torah), the Prophets (Nevi'im), and the Writings (Ketuvim). Jesus reflects this shape in Luke 24:44 when He speaks of "the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms," the Psalms standing for the Writings.

sa.prompt: By what marks were Old Testament books recognized as Scripture?
sa.model: Books were recognized by marks such as prophetic authorship or authority, consistency with what God had already revealed, and reception by the covenant community over generations. Recognition was a settling over time, not a manufacturing by decree.

sa.prompt: How does Luke 11:51 ("from Abel to Zechariah") show the extent of the canon Jesus received?
sa.model: Abel is the first martyr in Genesis and Zechariah the last in Chronicles, which stands last in the Hebrew order. By naming "from Abel to Zechariah," Jesus draws a line around the whole span of the Hebrew Scriptures — much as we might say "from Genesis to Revelation" — showing the canon was already fixed.

sa.prompt: What does Josephus tell us about the state of the Hebrew canon by the first century?
sa.model: Writing about AD 95, Josephus testified that the Hebrew books were a fixed number, written between Moses and Artaxerxes, to which nothing had been added and which no one dared alter — he counted twenty-two. This is outside testimony that the canon was already closed and known in the first century, not still open.

sa.prompt: Explain why the Old Testament is counted as 22, 24, or 39 books.
sa.model: These numbers are the same books counted differently. The Hebrew tradition reached 22 or 24 by treating the twelve Minor Prophets as one book and joining Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, and Ezra-Nehemiah each as single books. English and Spanish Bibles split these out to reach 39. Nothing is added or removed — only grouped differently.

sa.prompt: What was the "Council of Jamnia," and why does the unit call it a camel worth refusing?
sa.model: It was long taught that a Jewish council at Jamnia closed the OT canon about AD 90, but that council is a nineteenth-century reconstruction, not an ancient record. What the rabbis at Yavneh actually discussed — whether books like Ecclesiastes "defile the hands" — assumes those books were already Scripture. It is a camel because it was swallowed on a teacher's word without checking.

sa.prompt: Why does correcting the Jamnia claim strengthen, rather than weaken, the conservative case?
sa.model: Because the Jamnia story actually places the canon's close late, in a Jewish council after Christ. Removing it does not lose ground — it gains it: the honest history is that the canon was recognized far earlier and needed no council to make it so. The more accurate account is the more conservative one.

sa.prompt: In what sense is the Old Testament the believer holds "the canon Jesus held"?
sa.model: The Old Testament in the believer's Bible is the Hebrew Scriptures that were already settled in Jesus' day — the very books He read, quoted as authoritative, and called unbreakable ("the Scripture cannot be broken"). Opening to Genesis, the Psalms, or Malachi, the believer holds what Jesus held.

sa.prompt: Restate this unit's method in your own words: how should we treat a familiar claim like the Jamnia council?
sa.model: A familiar claim should not be believed simply because it is familiar or came from a trusted teacher. We test it against the evidence and follow where the evidence leads — even when that means correcting a long-held belief. Here that discipline led to a more honest and more conservative conclusion.
